The one overlap is **required points served**: the team check counts them too, because an owner that leaves a set-out point out of its own requirements would otherwise be caught by nobody, and unserved points were the most common failure in the measured runs without a coordinator. The model is settled only when both checks pass.
5. **Whoever finds an issue writes it, at the place.** Any agent, owner or coordinator, that finds a problem in or with someone's objects leaves a note of kind `issue` at that spot, addressed to the owner of the object that has to change, with from, to, kind and status. It never fixes another owner's objects and does not wait for the coordinator's turn. The owner replies when the fix is in its file; the author closes the note. Notes are open to all: the team check lists open notes by addressee, and the coordinator reads every one each turn.
6. **Rebuild only what moved, and look before you save.** One script per assembly; after a new revision, rerun only the assemblies the change or a note touches. Before saving a re-routed run, check it against the other owners' files as last saved (`others()`) and against your own requirements check. In the measured runs, owners re-routing after a change caused nearly all the faults that followed, often breaking something new each round.
7. **Nothing is settled while a note is open.** Every owner answers each note addressed to it in the turn it reads it (a fix and a reply, or a reply saying why not) and closes its own notes once answered. The coordinator never reports the model settled while any note is open, its own rulings included; the team check enforces this. Four of the six measured runs that did not end coordinated were models with no faults left and notes still open, and in two of them the coordinator had declared the model settled anyway.
8. **Reissue the set-out at most once a round, and only when shares change.** Every reissue raises the revision, and every owner file, stamp, opening request and opening built to the old one goes stale until its owner rebuilds. Collect all of a round's share changes and rulings, then reissue once; a ruling that moves no share is a note, not a reissue. Save the reissued set-out before running the team check, or the check reads the old revision. (A measured coordinator reissued five times in five rounds and left 16 to 22 stale references in every check.)

## Procedure

1. **Preflight, every agent, before anything else.** Follow [rhino-setup](../rhino-setup/SKILL.md): the Rhino tools are present, a document is open, its units are known. Then load the helpers (step 4) and run `print(ns["preflight"]())`: it names the shared folder, whether the set-out exists, any owner file that is missing, and whether the open document is your own file. Stop and give the user the exact missing action while `problems` is not empty; do not build, review or rule until every agent's preflight is clear. **The coordinator's preflight does not wait for the set-out:** before one exists it is clear, and its `next` says to save the open document as `setout.3dm` in the shared folder and write the set-out (step 3). An owner's preflight stays blocked until the set-out exists; an owner whose own file is not saved yet is told where to save it.
2. **Set up, with the user, once.** Agree the shared folder, the owners and their files, and the host owner. Collect every value the owners will need in one round of questions, so no owner has to ask the user.
3. **Write the set-out** in `setout.3dm` (coordinator's document): `write_setout(...)`, one point per required point on `Setout::Points`, and `share(...)` for each owner's share of every space more than one owner needs. Leave no shared space unallocated where two owners' routes could meet.
   - **Levels come from the host's floors:** `levels_from(<host objects>)` gives one level per floor or slab, at its top, named as the floor is (`Cellar`, `F1`, ... `Roof`). Pass that list as `levels`. Ceilings and joist undersides are not levels: put them in `numbers`. (In the first measured series with this skill, before `levels_from`, none of the three coordinators' set-outs matched the host's six floor levels; with it, all three matched every level.)
   - **Size each share to the runs it holds,** not to the whole zone: its count of runs times the owner's minimum size plus working clearance. A share is room for runs, not the ceiling.
   - **Declare every shared space and who passes through it:** `"shared_spaces": [{"name": "Shaft", "box": [...], "owners": [...]}]` in the set-out data, for every opening the host leaves for runs to pass a wall or floor (a shaft, a slot or gap in a wall). An owner passes through it when its source and some of its points lie on different sides of that wall or floor and this is the way through; list every such owner, and give each a share inside the space. (In a measured run the coordinator gave the one gap in a cellar wall to one owner, though all three owners' mains had to pass it.)
   - **Keep shares clear of the host's solids** (walls, slabs, joists), except through the host's openings such as the shaft.
   - **Where an owner's run must cross the host** (a line set through a wall, a pipe through a floor), draw that piece as its own short share with `share(..., crossing=True)`, just around the run. A crossing share may sit in host solids only inside a host opening or the owner's own opening request; `check_setout()` and the team check refuse it anywhere else. The owner keeps the crossing piece in that share, so its own check passes at the crossing, and requests the opening as usual.
   - **Run `check_setout()` and fix every problem before the owners' first turn,** and again after every `issue()`. The same check also runs by itself: `issue()` returns it with the new revision, and every team check includes it (`setout_gaps`) and refuses `Team: settled` while any problem remains, so shares redrawn mid-run cannot leave an overlap behind. It refuses levels off the host's floors, host floors with no level, a share running into a host solid, and overlapping shares, and warns about a share far larger than its owner's runs. When the host is not an owner (a given shell nobody writes), name its file in the set-out data as `"host_file": "<file>.3dm"`: the re-check in `issue()`, `check_setout()` and the team check then always read the host as last saved, including geometry a change adds. Without `host_file`, they use the one other `.3dm` in the shared folder if there is exactly one.
4. **Rounds are driven by the user.** Nobody else starts a round. In a round, every owner takes a turn on the others' files as last saved, then saves; then the coordinator takes its turn. When a change has been issued, the coordinator's turn comes first in that round. Each turn, load the helpers by path from the folder you read this `SKILL.md` from, which belongs to the installed plugin version:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-agent-team.py"
ns = {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_TEAM": {"folder": "<shared folder>", "me": "<owner name or coordinator>", "round": 3}}
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), ns)
print(ns["summary"]())
```

5. **Coordinator turn: read everything.** Run the team check with `"AS_MODE": "check"` and `"write": True` in `AS_TEAM`, and read every open note, not only those addressed to you (`summary()` lists them as `all_open_notes`).
6. **The team check writes the fault notes; you keep the judgment.** Every round, run `ns["post_fault_notes"]()`, then `save()`, then the team check with `"write": True`. The helper turns every fault on the check's list into one `issue` note at the object, addressed to the one owner who must move, marked as written by the check (`by: "team-check"`, with a `fault_key`): clashes (the share decides who moves, then the priority order), share breaks, runs through the host without an opening, requests the host has not answered, unserved points, failed `within` checks, and notes left unanswered for a round. It writes no second note for a fault whose note is still open, and closes its own notes once the check no longer lists the fault. **Do not retype faults as notes yourself:** whoever detects a problem most reliably documents it. In the measured barn run the coordinator's own review covered 10 of 27 faults and raised 15 wrong issues; a scripted reviewer raising exactly the check's list missed none. Your review keeps only what needs judgment:
   - **disputes:** an owner replies that the other owner should move instead; decide under step 7 with a `ruling`;
   - **set-out changes:** a share that does not work, or a fault no move within the shares can clear;
   - **the architect's change order** (a `change` note), under invariant 2;
   - stale items the check marks `for_coordinator` in `stale_by_owner` (left stale for a round after their reissue).

   You never model.
7. **Decide what owners cannot settle:** who moves when two owners each say the other should, and anything that changes the set-out (a `change` note, a share that does not work). Rule with one `ruling` note to the owner who moves. A `request` for an open design value that only the user can answer goes to the user once, in one question with the others.
8. **Finish** only when the team check prints `Team: settled`: no fault, every point served, every owner's own check current, no note open, and no version mismatch. A version mismatch means an owner's machine runs a different Arch Studio release or helper than the coordinator's: ask that person to update to the coordinator's release (see [Installing for a team](#installing-for-a-team)), then have them run their check, `stamp()` and `save()` again. If it does not settle within the rounds the user allowed, stop and report the check's list.

## Installing for a team

Every person's machine runs the helpers from its own installed plugin, so every machine needs the Arch Studio plugin (`as`), and everyone must be on **the same release** before a team session. `stamp()` and `write_setout()` record in each file the plugin version and a fingerprint of the helpers (this skill's script and rhino-model's check scripts, so a locally edited copy shows too), and the team check refuses `Team: settled` until every owner's file matches the coordinator's set-out.

- **Install on every machine:** `claude plugin marketplace add AlpacaLabsLLC/skills-for-architects`, then `claude plugin install as@skills-for-architects`. For the Rhino AI panel, install at user scope (the default), since the panel reads the user's settings.
- **Claude Code, shared project:** the firm can commit the marketplace and the enabled plugin in the project's `.claude/settings.json`, under `extraKnownMarketplaces` (`"skills-for-architects": {"source": {"source": "github", "repo": "AlpacaLabsLLC/skills-for-architects"}}`) and `enabledPlugins` (`"as@skills-for-architects": true`). Claude Code registers the marketplace once each teammate trusts the folder; enabling the plugin there does not install it, so each teammate still runs the install command above.
- **Several sessions in one IDE (Orca or another terminal host):** see [Running the team in Orca](README.md#running-the-team-in-orca-or-any-ide-terminal-host).
- **Before a team session:** everyone updates to the same release (`claude plugin marketplace update skills-for-architects`, then `claude plugin update as@skills-for-architects`), and each agent's `summary()` shows its `plugin` and `helper` so they can be compared.

## Working in a team

Read this part if you are an owner. Build your part with [rhino-model](../rhino-model/SKILL.md), as its section *When a set-out exists* describes. Each turn: `summary()` first; read notes addressed to you; if the set-out revision is newer than your stamp, read its `change` and handle it as a brief change; build only in your shares or in space the set-out leaves to you; `request_opening(...)` where a run of yours crosses the host's elements; answer every note addressed to you this turn and close your own notes once answered; **clear your own stale items this turn without waiting for a note:** run the team check read only (`team_check = ns["check"]` on the shared folder, without `write`) and act on your entries in `stale_by_owner`. `re-stamp` means the item still holds: `stamp()` re-stamps your requests that still sit in your shares or a host opening (`restamp_requests()` does only that), and returns `requests_restamped` and `requests_to_rebuild`; `summary()` shows `my_stale_requests`. `rebuild` means what it was built to moved: rebuild it, check, and stamp. A reissue that did not touch your shares, points, levels or datum leaves your work current; nothing of yours is listed then; when you see a problem with another owner's objects, `note(<that owner>, ..., kind="issue")` at the place, and leave their objects alone; answer issue notes addressed to you with `kind="reply"` once fixed, or reply saying why not if you disagree; `note("coordinator", ..., kind="request")` only for open design values and for candidate lessons; run your own requirements check after the last geometry change; then `stamp()` and `save()`. `stamp()` returns its status against the set-out as it is now: report it as given, and if it says **stale**, your file is not current, whatever you stamped; read the set-out's `change`, rebuild what moved, check and stamp again. The helpers refuse to write when the open document is not your file.

## Report

Open with the team check's `Team:` line exactly as printed. Then: the set-out revision and its last change, the rounds run, the issue notes you wrote and closed this round, per owner its own check status and what changed this round, open notes, and what is not checked (below). Complete under the [completion contract](../../docs/completion-reporting.md).

## What the team check can and cannot prove

It reads the saved files only. It accepts an owner's own check only when the stored result passed, was run on the file's current requirements revision, and carries a geometry fingerprint (object ids, layers and bounding boxes) equal to the saved file's; an owner whose file changed after its check fails. Notes are left out of the fingerprint. Clashes are shared volume between two owners' solids (touching is not a clash); share and connection checks use bounding boxes, so runs should be straight along x, y or z. A required point is served when a run of its system touches it and connects, piece touching piece, back to that system's source. It checks coordination and modelling practice, never codes, sizes, slopes, clearances or engineering.

## Not tested yet

- **Owners using rhino-model through Rhino's own connection.** The skills were loaded only through the test harness: on a three-owner house, two series of three team runs against three of owners alone, and on the five-owner barn, where one of four Sonnet runs settled ([evidence](references/evidence.md)).
- **Real sessions.** Every measured run used headless documents and a script that ran the rounds, saved, reopened and measured. Several agent sessions on window documents, a person driving rounds, and `save()` have not been run.
- **Recovering from a change in one round.** With the change delivered as a note to the coordinator, who went first that round, no setup recovered in the change round; 2 to 4 rounds where it recovered at all.
- **Agents belonging to different people,** more than five owners, and larger models.

## Out of scope

Agents editing the same file, live sync between sessions, rendering, structural or MEP design, and code compliance.

skills.name: rhino-axon
skills.desc: The view for an axonometric sheet from a Rhino 9 model: camera and projection, exclusions and cut-away crop, hidden-line occlusion, joint and detail-cut selection, and the building lock, handing linework and cut faces to rhino-thinline. Use when the user asks for an axonometric, axon sheet or exploded axon from a Rhino model; read rhino-thinline too, for the conventions. Not for coloured images or renders, and it never edits the model to get a view.
skills.body:
---
name: rhino-axon
description: "The view for an axonometric sheet from a Rhino 9 model: camera and projection, exclusions and cut-away crop, hidden-line occlusion, joint and detail-cut selection, and the building lock, handing linework and cut faces to rhino-thinline. Use when the user asks for an axonometric, axon sheet or exploded axon from a Rhino model; read rhino-thinline too, for the conventions. Not for coloured images or renders, and it never edits the model to get a view."
---

# /as:rhino-axon

Before acting, read the [host contract](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md), this component's [declaration](host-contract.json) (`skill:rhino-axon`) and the mode profiles it references in the [shared catalog](../../corpus/host-contracts.json). Declarations are requirements, not proof of access or permission.

<!-- architecture-studio:harness-compatibility -->
Use the [host adapter](../../docs/host-adapters.md) for native invocation. Requires Rhino 9 with an open document and its `run_python` tool. **Plugin-only:** the view and its checks use `scripts/as-axon.py` from the installed plugin's folder ([Rhino skill helpers](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md#rhino-skill-helpers)); through hosted MCP instruction delivery this skill is not available. If you cannot find this skill's folder on disk, stop and tell the user to install the plugin. In the Rhino AI panel, there is no Skill tool: read this file and its references by path with `run_python`.

## Outcome

An axonometric on a layout in the open document: the view chosen, projected and drawn as linework, its details cut from the real joints, and the building unchanged. The sheet itself (weights, hatch, annotation, layout, the request record and the PDF) follows [rhino-thinline](../rhino-thinline/SKILL.md); read that skill too, and report under both.

## Invariants

1. **True black and white comes from hidden-line vectors,** not from a line-based display mode. The output is static: after a model change, regenerate it.
2. **A detail bubble is a locator.** Its leader lands on the real joint, and it is cut from that same member.
3. **The sheet never edits the building.** Draw from the model as it is: no deleting, moving, trimming or rebuilding building geometry to make a leader or a view work. `setup_sheet` records the building and `check_sheet` fails if any of it was changed or removed. If a leader cannot reach a joint, pick another joint or move the detail; if the model itself is wrong, say so and stop.
4. **Leave out or cut away in the drawing only.** `exclude` and `crop` act on in-memory copies; the model is never trimmed to show what is behind.
5. **Hand linework, not choices.** This skill decides what is seen and draws it on the page under its own layer roots; rhino-thinline's conventions read it from there and never move the camera ([the handoff](references/views.md#the-linework-handoff)).
6. **Never change a check's threshold, and never delete a failure record or request to pass a check;** report what could not be placed.
7. **One sheet per document.** `setup_sheet` refuses a second sheet in a document that already holds one, because the request, building and main drawing records are the document's, not the layout's. Tell the user, and draw the new sheet in another document that holds the model and no sheet; never delete the first sheet's records.

## Procedure

Read the [lessons](#lessons) after setup and before asking; write them after the report.

1. **Setup and ask** as in [rhino-thinline](../rhino-thinline/SKILL.md) steps 1 and 2: one `ask_user` batch for drawing, scale, sheet size, details and title text. Without `ask_user`, ask the same in chat, as thinline says.
2. **Load the library** by file path. It loads rhino-thinline's library into the same namespace first, so one load gives both. Build the path from the folder you read this `SKILL.md` from, which belongs to the installed plugin version; never hard-code it or reuse one from an earlier version:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-axon.py"
S = {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P}
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), S)
```

3. **Build in this order** with one script per step, following [views](references/views.md) and thinline's [sheets](../rhino-thinline/references/sheets.md): `setup_sheet` for the layout and parallel detail, with its target document active (a headless document need not be); main linework, with every owner's top layer as the source when the model was assembled from several files; annotation and callouts; details, each with `cut_detail`; title block and table. Annotation goes after linework, so it draws on top.
   - **When a label cannot be placed** (`place_label` refuses every point), never cut the building away for it: give it other points on the part's visible outside edge, shorten or drop the label, and report any label left unplaced. A cut-away is for showing a joint, not for making room for text.
   - **When a detail cannot be placed** (`place_locator` refuses every point and `check_sheet` names it), the joint is inside the drawing. Never edit, trim or delete the model to clear a path. Instead:
     1. Draw a cut-away with `main_linework(crop=(x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1))`, ending the box at the edge of the window, door or joint you want to show, so that joint sits on the drawing's outline. The cut-away's cut faces are drawn in outline, not hatched; only details hatch their cut faces.
     2. Try the other view side (for example `direction` with x negated), so the cut face of the cut-away turns away from the viewer and the joint becomes the drawing's edge.
     3. Give the placers several points along the part's visible outside edge, nearest the details.
4. **Review** as in rhino-thinline step 5.
5. **Check the sheet** with `S["check_sheet"]`, passing the main linework root, the main detail and its scale, and the drawing field. Loaded from here it is the full check: rhino-thinline's conventions and this view in one list. Then export and run the PDF check as in rhino-thinline step 6.

## Lessons

This skill learns locally. Before planning, read its lessons and the firm rules, and rhino-thinline's; at the end of every run, write what the run learned about the view here and about conventions there. The folder is the one the Arch Studio startup line names; the tags, the privacy rule and promotion are in [lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md), read once per session.

```python
P = "<absolute path of the skills folder, the parent of this skill's folder>/as-rhino-lessons.py"
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_MODE": "read", "AS_SKILL": "rhino-axon", "AS_LESSONS_DIR": "<lessons folder from the startup line>"})
```

Follow every firm rule, and name each lesson you apply in the report. To write, use `"AS_MODE": "write"` with `AS_LESSONS`, `AS_PRIVATE` and `__rhino_doc__`, then `"offer"`. Each lesson declares its kind: `practice` (modeling practice) or `preference` (the user's own, with what the user said). Never save a design, architectural or engineering rule you inferred; mention it to the user instead ([lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md)). A firm rule is written only with `"promote"`, after the user said yes in `ask_user`. Never edit the checker, its tests or answer keys to apply a lesson.

## Report

rhino-thinline's report, plus: the scale read back, what was excluded or cut away and why, each detail's joint, and any label or detail that could not be placed. Name the lessons applied and written, or "none". Complete under the [completion contract](../../docs/completion-reporting.md).

## Out of scope

Editing the model to get a view, coloured images ([rhino-batch-image-export](../rhino-batch-image-export/SKILL.md)), and the drawing conventions themselves ([rhino-thinline](../rhino-thinline/SKILL.md)). A ghosted envelope for closed buildings is not built yet.

Declarations are requirements, not proof of access or permission.

If you cannot find this skill's folder on disk, stop and tell the user to install the plugin. In the Rhino AI panel, there is no Skill tool: read this file and its reference by path with `run_python`.

## Outcome

A folder of PNGs the user named, in which every file was read back and matched the requested mode, and a reply opening with the script's `Export:` line.

## Invariants

1. **Verify the exported file, not the viewport.** A batch came out in colour while the viewport showed the requested mode. The batch fails when any file does not match, and the failed files are moved aside with a `FAILED-` prefix.
2. **Name the mode in the capture.** Set it on the viewport and pass it to `CaptureToBitmap`; never rely on the mode already showing.
3. **Capture only by script.** Never use the capture tool's `cameraLocation`, `target` or `view` arguments, which blank or rewrite views. Set the camera in `run_python` and let the view settle ([display](references/display.md)).
4. **Leave the document as found.** Layer visibility, camera and display mode are restored after every batch, and the batch fails if layers, materials or the object count changed.
5. **No temporary colours or materials.** A temporary red reached delivered images. If one is unavoidable, restore and verify it before capturing.

## Procedure

Read the [lessons](#lessons) after setup and before asking; write them after the report.

1. **Setup.** If the Rhino tools are absent, follow [rhino-setup](../rhino-setup/SKILL.md) for the user action. List modes with `"AS_MODE": "modes"`.
2. **Ask** in one `ask_user` batch only what is open: mode, views, layouts, image size, output folder. Each question carries what it asks about, with your proposal as the first option ("Keep 1/4\" = 1'-0\""), since the question pane covers the chat; never refer to text shown behind it. Where `ask_user` is not available (an agent connected to Rhino from outside it), ask the same questions in chat, with the same options, and end the turn.
3. **Export** by file path. Build the path from the folder you read this `SKILL.md` from, which belongs to the installed plugin version; never hard-code it or reuse one from an earlier version:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-batch-image-export.py"
SPEC = {"out": "<folder>", "mode": "Arctic", "size": [3840, 2160], "shots": [{"name": "option-a-birdseye", "direction": "birdseye", "layers": ["Building::Option A"]}]}
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_MODE": "export", "AS_EXPORT": SPEC})
```

## Out of scope

Photorealistic rendering, installing display modes, and interior views. For black and white vector sheets use [rhino-thinline](../rhino-thinline/SKILL.md).

# /as:rhino-bom

Before acting, read the [host contract](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md), this component's [declaration](host-contract.json) (`skill:rhino-bom`) and the mode profiles it references in the [shared catalog](../../corpus/host-contracts.json). Declarations are requirements, not proof of access or permission.

<!-- architecture-studio:harness-compatibility -->
Use the [host adapter](../../docs/host-adapters.md) for native invocation. Requires Rhino 9 with an open document and its `run_python` tool. **Plugin-only:** the quantities and their reconciliation use `scripts/as-bom.py` from the installed plugin's folder ([Rhino skill helpers](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md#rhino-skill-helpers)); through hosted MCP instruction delivery this skill is not available. If you cannot find this skill's folder on disk, stop and tell the user to install the plugin. In the Rhino AI panel, there is no Skill tool: read this file and its references by path with `run_python`.

## Outcome

One CSV per layout under a folder the user chose, and a reply opening with the script's `BOM:` line, in which the object total reconciles and nothing was silently left out.

## Invariants

1. **Everything in the model, by default.** Offer the full scope first. A shorter scope is the user's choice, stated in `covers`.
2. **Reconcile to the object count.** Every object lands in one line or in `excluded` with a reason. One object with no line fails the run, and no CSV is written.
3. **Quantities depend on names.** The script reads the object names and layers that [as-rhino-model](../rhino-model/SKILL.md) gives every object. A generic or missing name loses the item, so fix the model's names rather than adding a catch-all rule.
4. **Every line states its source:** measured from the model, calculated, or assumed, with the reason in the same column.
5. **List what is not counted, with the reason.** Fittings, traps, valves, fasteners, footings and rebar are usual cases. An unmentioned omission reads as zero. `not_counted` is required.
6. **Cut lengths are firm; purchase counts depend on assumed stock.** Keep them in separate lines. Identical and near-identical members share one line with a count and a cut-length range; the CSV's cut schedule keeps every exact length, and nesting uses them.
7. **A count does not validate the thing counted.** Mark hardware `to_engineer`.

## Procedure

Read the [lessons](#lessons) after setup and before asking; write them after the report.

1. **Read the document** with one script: units, layers, and whether the model's parent layer exists. If the Rhino tools are absent, follow [rhino-setup](../rhino-setup/SKILL.md) for the user action.
2. **Ask** only what the model cannot answer, in one `ask_user` batch: scope (default everything), layouts, stock lengths, sheet sizes, waste, output folder. Each question carries what it asks about, with your proposal as the first option ("Keep 1/4\" = 1'-0\""), since the question pane covers the chat; never refer to text shown behind it. Where `ask_user` is not available (an agent connected to Rhino from outside it), ask the same questions in chat, with the same options, and end the turn.
3. **List the names**: run with `"AS_MODE": "names"`. Every name it prints needs a rule or an exclusion.
4. **Write the specification** from [quantities](references/quantities.md), which lists the measures and the choice of measure by geometry.
5. **Run** by file path. Build the path from the folder you read this `SKILL.md` from, which belongs to the installed plugin version; never hard-code it or reuse one from an earlier version:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-bom.py"
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_MODE": "check", "AS_BOM": SPEC})
```

   `"check"` reconciles and writes nothing. Fix every unclassified name and every object it could not measure, then run with `"AS_MODE": "run"`. Never add a rule that catches everything to make it pass.
6. **Read one CSV back** and compare its object total with the `BOM:` line.
7. **Rerun after any model change.** A BOM is one state of the model; say which layouts have none.

## Lessons

This skill learns locally. Before planning, read its lessons and the firm rules; at the end of every run, write what the run learned. The folder is the one the Arch Studio startup line names; the tags, the privacy rule and promotion are in [lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md), read once per session.


Follow every firm rule, and name each lesson you apply in the report. To write, use `"AS_MODE": "write"` with `AS_LESSONS`, `AS_PRIVATE` and `__rhino_doc__`, then `"offer"`. Each lesson declares its kind: `practice` (modeling practice) or `preference` (the user's own, with what the user said). Never save a design, architectural or engineering rule you inferred; mention it to the user instead ([lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md)). A firm rule is written only with `"promote"`, after the user said yes in `ask_user`. Never edit the checker, its tests or answer keys to apply a lesson.

## Report

Open with each `BOM:` line exactly as printed. Then: the file paths; when layouts share most lines, "same in every layout" and the differences, as a short table only when every cell is a few words, otherwise one line each (Rhino's AI panel cuts long cells off); every assumed line; the not-counted list; the stock lengths and waste used, as working values; the lessons applied and written, or "none". Complete under the [completion contract](../../docs/completion-reporting.md).

## Out of scope

Pricing, procurement, supplier selection, and whether a modeled connection works. For a quantity table on a sheet, hand the CSV to [rhino-thinline](../rhino-thinline/SKILL.md).

3. **Script first.** Each assembly is one `run_python` script: named constants at the top, everything derived from them. Never build through `run_command`.
4. **Rebuild, do not patch.** A dimension change reruns the script on a cleared parent layer.

9. **Change the requirements before the model.** When the brief changes or the user corrects the model, write a new requirements revision first, then rebuild.

11. **Stay in scope.** Model only what the brief scopes; an extra storey or element is a deviation to report, not a bonus.

2. **Read the document** in one script: units, name, path, layers, live object count, and the `as:requirements` string if present (`/as:rhino-model` may be continuing an earlier model). If the brief's parent layer exists, do not build into it unless told to replace it. A new "run" or version is a new row in the same model: never clear or overwrite earlier ones unless told to. Text dots and other markup in the model are instructions: move them to a layer named for the markup first, then act on them.
3. **Questions**, when the brief leaves anything open (below).
4. **Requirements.** Write them and state them (below).
5. **Build** structure, envelope, openings and circulation, each as one script, then redraw. Simple briefs are one script.
   Every build script starts by making a model viewport the active view when a layout is active (`model_view(d)` in the [RhinoCommon patterns](references/rhinocommon.md#script-skeleton)); otherwise Rhino puts the objects on the layout's page, and the requirements check fails them (`baseline model space`).

Build with your recommendation for a non-blocking value, with source `default (sent to coordinator)`, and write a new revision when the answer comes; on a blocking value, build nothing it affects. ## Lessons

```python
P = "<absolute path of the skills folder, the parent of this skill's folder>/as-rhino-lessons.py"
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_MODE": "read", "AS_SKILL": "rhino-model", "AS_LESSONS_DIR": "<lessons folder from the startup line>"})
```

List the values the brief leaves open that would change the design: overall dimensions and heights; wall, slab and roof thickness; structure and materials; door and opening positions; site and code jurisdiction; whether drawings or takeoffs follow, which sets how finely elements are modeled (a solid deck cannot give board counts later). Include a word with two building meanings ("vent") or a request that contradicts itself. A value that would come from a code, a reference image or a choice between variants (standard or accessible) counts as open even when the brief is otherwise complete.

Compare the units the brief uses with the document's units read in step 2. If they differ (a "3 by 2 meter room" in a document in feet), make that the first question, proposing to keep the document's units and convert the brief's values.

Before asking, check that the recommendations fit together (a door head under a raked plate, a roof against an existing wall); recommendations that conflict are not a recommendation. A value that barely affects the design is a stated assumption.

**Every question carries what it asks about.** In the Rhino AI panel, `ask_user` opens a pane over the chat, so never ask about something shown in the chat behind it ("the table above", "these values"): put the value in the question and its options.

1. **One `ask_user` call with one question.** Its text names every recommended value, as short label and value pairs: "Build with these recommendations? Footprint: 12 × 16 ft; wall height: 8 ft; roof: 6:12 gable; walls: 2×6 at 16 in; slab: 4 in; door: 3 × 6 ft 8 in on the south gable". The pane shows the question as plain text, with no line breaks and no formatting, and does not scroll, so use semicolons, no reasons, and keep it to a few lines. The options are exactly "Use all recommended" and "Go through each one by one". Put no other question in that call, and end the turn. If the values will not fit in a few lines (more than about eight), skip this step and go to step 2.
2. **"Go through each one by one" goes straight to the per-row form.** One `ask_user` call with one question per value, most consequential first, one decision each (wall, floor and roof thickness are three questions). Each question names its value ("Wall thickness: 2×6 studs with sheathing"); the first option is "Keep <recommended value>" ("Keep 6 in"), then any real alternative. The panel adds Other, for the user's own value, so do not add it. `ask_user` takes every question in one call and shows them one page at a time, with no limit on their number. Never ask which values to change first.

- **The answers end the questioning:** "Use all recommended", or the per-row answers. Write the requirements and build. Ask nothing more about design values in this run. If a value turns out not to work while building (a conflict you missed), apply the smallest change that keeps the brief and the firm rules, write it as a new revision with `change`, and name it in the report as a changed recommendation; do not ask. The only questions still allowed are a new blocking question (as defined above) and, at the end, promotion.
- **Where `ask_user` is not available** (an agent connected to Rhino from outside it), show the recommendations in chat, one per line ("Wall thickness: 6 in, 2×6 studs with sheathing (why)"), ask once in chat with the same two choices, "Use all recommended" or "Go through each one by one", and end the turn; for the second, ask each value in chat with its recommendation to keep. Answers that keep a recommendation are source `user (accepted recommendation)`.

Skip the questions when nothing open remains or the user said to proceed ("use defaults", "use recommended", "just build"), and list the recommendations as assumptions. Do not ask about what the brief, the document, the user or a firm rule already settles. Values the user set or changed are source `user`; accepted recommendations are source `user (accepted recommendation)`.

**End of run.** Do not ask whether to save: leave the document unsaved unless the user asked for a save, and say so in the report. The only end-of-run question is promoting the user's own preferences to firm rules, written in plain words as [lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md) sets out; never offer a lesson about tools, scripts or checks. When no candidate qualifies, ask nothing. Promotion is never covered by "Use all recommended".

## Requirements

Requirements live in the document, as JSON in the document string `as:requirements`, so they travel with the .3dm and the requirements check can measure against them. The format is the checker's: every check type is listed at the top of [as-check-model.py](scripts/as-check-model.py). Use `extent` for code ranges and one-sided limits ("16-18 in", "54 in min"), `clear` for clearances that must stay free, and `heights`, `objects` and `layers` for the rest. Add:

- `brief`: the brief, in the user's words.
- `sources`: one source per check, keyed by the check name as the requirements check prints it (`extent Seat`, `layer Walls`, `clear Walls`, `units`).
- `stated`: requirements the checks cannot measure (a product specification, a strength, something not modeled), each as one short line.
- `change`: why this revision exists; required from revision 2 ("brief changed: ...", "user correction: ...").
- `code`: when a value comes from a code, the jurisdiction, the code used, and `adopted`, `stand-in` or `none` ([checks](references/checks.md)).

For an envelope, a window or a door, add `proportion` for sealant joints, `cover` for cladding and flashing around each opening, `bears` for trim and jambs on a sill, `clash` for each flashing against the barrier, sheathing and cladding it laps, and `hardware` with `clash` for hinges; model flashing and membranes as closed thin solids and list their layers in `closed`, because `clash` skips open surfaces ([elements](references/elements.md)).

**Where values come from**, in order: the brief; what the user said in this session; a template in [references/requirements](references/requirements/) for the element (for example [toilet](references/requirements/toilet.json)), which gives values in a local frame with sources and variants to convert to world coordinates; then [elements](references/elements.md) for building elements; then defaults, labelled as defaults. When the brief names a code (ADA, IPC, a local code), cite the section for each value. A template value with a `verified` date was checked against the code text it cites: cite its section and edition, and do not call it unverified. A code value without one, including any you supply yourself, is a working value: say it is to be verified against the adopted code text. Use the edition the brief or project names. This skill's templates hold only the US codes they cite, and there is no code text for any other jurisdiction (for example, Example County). Ask for the local code as a blocking question; never supply its values from memory. When none is available, a foreign code is a stand-in: set `code` to say so, and the check reports it on every run.

**Write them** through the checker's write mode (`P` is built as in [Running the requirements check](#running-the-requirements-check)), which numbers the revision, keeps earlier revisions in `as:requirements-history`, refuses requirements without a `brief` (or, from revision 2, a `change`), lists checks with no source, and prints what changed:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-check.py"
REQ = {"units": "Inches", "parent": "Bath", "brief": "...", "change": "...", "sources": {...}, "stated": [...], "extent": {...}}
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_MODE": "write", "AS_REQUIREMENTS": REQ})
```

Never write `as:requirements` with `SetString` directly. Start a new revision from the stored one (read it, edit it, write it) so nothing earlier is lost silently.

**State them.** Show the requirements in the reply, one per line ("Footprint: 12 × 16 ft, to the outside of the walls (brief)"), then build in the same turn. The answers are the confirmation; do not ask again.

**When the brief changes or the user corrects the model,** write the new revision first (with `change` naming what changed and the source the user gave), show what the write printed as changed, then rebuild and check. A correction that adds an element adds its requirements, not just its geometry.

### When the form changes

A form can change with no word from the user: a proportion corrected against a reference image, a failure fixed by moving geometry. After any such change, work out again every count and spacing recorded in a `derived` note.

- If a derived value would change, write a new revision first, with `change` naming the form change ("form change: bay width 3.6 to 3.2") and the new `derived` note, then rebuild from the same layout rule that produced the count. The check lists this revision as written after geometry existed. That is accurate: record it in `as:run-notes`, and name the change in the reply as a changed recommendation.
- Never pick a count or spacing so that the model still meets the old requirement. A passing check on a pinned count measures nothing.
- Only derived values move this way. A value from the brief or the user stays until the user changes it.

The check can warn but cannot prove this. It flags a `layers` entry with a `derived` note when that layer's overall size has moved by more than 1% since the revision was first measured, and the flag reaches the `Check notes` line. Recompute the count: write a new revision if it changed, or record in `as:run-notes` that it did not; never show the flag to the user. It cannot see a form change made before the first

Build with your recommendation for a non-blocking value, with source `default (sent to coordinator)`, and write a new revision when the answer comes; on a blocking value, build nothing it affects. Write lessons as usual, but instead of the end-of-run promotion question, send candidate lessons to the coordinator as a note, so they are not lost.
5. **Rebuild only what moved.** Invariant 4 holds per assembly: one script per assembly, and after a new revision rerun only the assemblies the change touches. Your parent layer is your owner's parent layer in the set-out (`Plumbing`, with children such as `Plumbing::Drain`).

## Lessons

This skill learns locally. Before planning, read its lessons and the firm rules; at the end of every run, write what the run learned. The folder is the one the Arch Studio startup line names; the tags, the privacy rule and promotion are in [lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md), read once per session.

```python
P = "<absolute path of the skills folder, the parent of this skill's folder>/as-rhino-lessons.py"
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_MODE": "read", "AS_SKILL": "rhino-model", "AS_LESSONS_DIR": "<lessons folder from the startup line>"})
```

Follow every firm rule. Name the firm rules and user preferences you apply in the reply (Report, item 6), and every other lesson you apply in `as:run-notes`. To write, use `"AS_MODE": "write"` with `AS_LESSONS`, `AS_PRIVATE` and `__rhino_doc__`, then `"offer"`. Each lesson declares its kind: `practice` (modeling practice) or `preference` (the user's own, with what the user said). Never save a design, architectural or engineering rule you inferred; mention it to the user instead ([lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md)). A firm rule is written only with `"promote"`, after the user said yes in `ask_user`. Never edit the checker, its tests or answer keys to apply a lesson.

## Questions

List the values the brief leaves open that would change the design: overall dimensions and heights; wall, slab and roof thickness; structure and materials; door and opening positions; site and code jurisdiction; whether drawings or takeoffs follow, which sets how finely elements are modeled (a solid deck cannot give board counts later). Include a word with two building meanings ("vent") or a request that contradicts itself. A value that would come from a code, a reference image or a choice between variants (standard or accessible) counts as open even when the brief is otherwise complete.

Compare the units the brief uses with the document's units read in step 2. If they differ (a "3 by 2 meter room" in a document in feet), make that the first question, proposing to keep the document's units and convert the brief's values.

Every routine design value is a recommendation, never a question of its own. Before asking, check that the recommendations fit together (a door head under a raked plate, a roof against an existing wall); recommendations that conflict are not a recommendation. A value that barely affects the design is a stated assumption.

**Every question carries what it asks about.** In the Rhino AI panel, `ask_user` opens a pane over the chat, so never ask about something shown in the chat behind it ("the table above", "these values"): put the value in the question and its options.

**Blocking questions come first, in their own call.** A question is blocking only when it cannot be defaulted: a units mismatch, a conflict with the document (it already holds another project's requirements or geometry), a contradiction in the brief, a destructive action (replacing or deleting work you did not create), or a code jurisdiction you have no text for. A design value is never blocking, even when it is phrased as a choice. If any blocking question exists, ask all of them in one `ask_user` call and end the turn; make the recommendations from the answers.

**Ask about the recommendations in two steps, each pane complete on its own.** You may first list the recommendations with their reasons in the reply, as reference.

1. **One `ask_user` call with one question.** Its text names every recommended value, as short label and value pairs: "Build with these recommendations? Footprint: 12 × 16 ft; wall height: 8 ft; roof: 6:12 gable; walls: 2×6 at 16 in; slab: 4 in; door: 3 × 6 ft 8 in on the south gable". The pane shows the question as plain text, with no line breaks and no formatting, and does not scroll, so use semicolons, no reasons, and keep it to a few lines. The options are exactly "Use all recommended" and "Go through each one by one". Put no other question in that call, and end the turn. If the values will not fit in a few lines (more than about eight), skip this step and go to step 2.
2. **"Go through each one by one" goes straight to the per-row form.** One `ask_user` call with one question per value, most consequential first, one decision each (wall, floor and roof thickness are three questions). Each question names its value ("Wall thickness: 2×6 studs with sheathing"); the first option is "Keep <recommended value>" ("Keep 6 in"), then any real alternative. The panel adds Other, for the user's own value, so do not add it. `ask_user` takes every question in one call and shows them one page at a time, with no limit on their number. Never ask which values to change first.

- **The answers end the questioning:** "Use all recommended", or the per-row answers. Write the requirements and build. Ask nothing more about design values in this run. If a value turns out not to work while building (a conflict you missed), apply the smallest change that keeps the brief and the firm rules, write it as a new revision with `change`, and name it in the report as a changed recommendation; do not ask. The only questions still allowed are a new blocking question (as defined above) and, at the end, promotion.
- **Where `ask_user` is not available** (an agent connected to Rhino from outside it), show the recommendations in chat, one per line ("Wall thickness: 6 in, 2×6 studs with sheathing (why)"), ask once in chat with the same two choices, "Use all recommended" or "Go through each one by one", and end the turn; for the second, ask each value in chat with its recommendation to keep. Answers that keep a recommendation are source `user (accepted recommendation)`.

Skip the questions when nothing open remains or the user said to proceed ("use defaults", "use recommended", "just build"), and list the recommendations as assumptions. Do not ask about what the brief, the document, the user or a firm rule already settles. Values the user set or changed are source `user`; accepted recommendations are source `user (accepted recommendation)`.

**End of run.** Do not ask whether to save: leave the document unsaved unless the user asked for a save, and say so in the report. The only end-of-run question is promoting the user's own preferences to firm rules, written in plain words as [lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md) sets out; never offer a lesson about tools, scripts or checks. When no candidate qualifies, ask nothing. Promotion is never covered by "Use all recommended".

## Requirements

Requirements live in the document, as JSON in the document string `as:requirements`, so they travel with the .3dm and the requirements check can measure against them. The format is the checker's: every check type is listed at the top of [as-check-model.py](scripts/as-check-model.py). Use `extent` for code ranges and one-sided limits ("16-18 in", "54 in min"), `clear` for clearances that must stay free, and `heights`, `objects` and `layers` for the rest. Add:

- `brief`: the brief, in the user's words.
- `sources`: one source per check, keyed by the check name as the requirements check prints it (`extent Seat`, `layer Walls`, `clear Walls`, `units`).
- `stated`: requirements the checks cannot measure (a product specification, a strength, something not modeled), each as one short line.
- `change`: why this revision exists; required from revision 2 ("brief changed: ...", "user correction: ...").
- `code`: when a value comes from a code, the jurisdiction, the code used, and `adopted`, `stand-in` or `none` ([checks](references/checks.md)).

Set them from the brief and the answers, before designing. Do not fit them to a design that already exists; the check flags a revision written once geometry exists. A revision that follows a design change is not fitting them: it stays, and the flag stays in the report. Derive `layers` counts from the layout constants and say how in `derived`; a very wide range is flagged, because 20 to 400 piers tells nothing. For a model with several systems, add `clash`, `network` and `hardware`, and declare intended connections in `intended` ([checks](references/checks.md)). For an envelope, a window or a door, add `proportion` for sealant joints, `cover` for cladding and flashing around each opening, `bears` for trim and jambs on a sill, `clash` for each flashing against the barrier, sheathing and cladding it laps, and `hardware` with `clash` for hinges; model flashing and membranes as closed thin solids and list their layers in `closed`, because `clash` skips open surfaces ([elements](references/elements.md)).

**Where values come from**, in order: the brief; what the user said in this session; a template in [references/requirements](references/requirements/) for the element (for example [toilet](references/requirements/toilet.json)), which gives values in a local frame with sources and variants to convert to world coordinates; then [elements](references/elements.md) for building elements; then defaults, labelled as defaults. When the brief names a code (ADA, IPC, a local code), cite the section for each value. A template value with a `verified` date was checked against the code text it cites: cite its section and edition, and do not call it unverified. A code value without one, including any you supply yourself, is a working value: say it is to be verified against the adopted code text. Use the edition the brief or project names. This skill's templates hold only the US codes they cite, and there is no code text for any other jurisdiction (for example, Example County). Ask for the local code as a blocking question; never supply its values from memory. When none is available, a foreign code is a stand-in: set `code` to say so, and the check reports it on every run.

**Write them** through the checker's write mode (`P` is built as in [Running the requirements check](#running-the-requirements-check)), which numbers the revision, keeps earlier revisions in `as:requirements-history`, refuses requirements without a `brief` (or, from revision 2, a `change`), lists checks with no source, and prints what changed:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-check.py"
REQ = {"units": "Inches", "parent": "Bath", "brief": "...", "change": "...", "sources": {...}, "stated": [...], "extent": {...}}
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_MODE": "write", "AS_REQUIREMENTS": REQ})
```

Never write `as:requirements` with `SetString` directly. Start a new revision from the stored one (read it, edit it, write it) so nothing earlier is lost silently.

**State them.** Show the requirements in the reply, one per line ("Footprint: 12 × 16 ft, to the outside of the walls (brief)"), then build in the same turn. The answers are the confirmation; do not ask again.

**When the brief changes or the user corrects the model,** write the new revision first (with `change` naming what changed and the source the user gave), show what the write printed as changed, then rebuild and check. A correction that adds an element adds its requirements, not just its geometry.

### When the form changes

A form can change with no word from the user: a proportion corrected against a reference image, a failure fixed by moving geometry. After any such change, work out again every count and spacing recorded in a `derived` note.

- If a derived value would change, write a new revision first, with `change` naming the form change ("form change: bay width 3.6 to 3.2") and the new `derived` note, then rebuild from the same layout rule that produced the count. The check lists this revision as written after geometry existed. That is accurate: record it in `as:run-notes`, and name the change in the reply as a changed recommendation.
- Never pick a count or spacing so that the model still meets the old requirement. A passing check on a pinned count measures nothing.
- Only derived values move this way. A value from the brief or the user stays until the user changes it.

The check can warn but cannot prove this. It flags a `layers` entry with a `derived` note when that layer's overall size has moved by more than 1% since the revision was first measured, and the flag reaches the `Check notes` line. Recompute the count: write a new revision if it changed, or record in `as:run-notes` that it did not; never show the flag to the user. It cannot see a form change made before the first check, a constant changed inside an unchanged extent, or a count without a `derived` note, and it cannot tell why a constant was set. The rule above still applies when no flag appears. A new revision clears the flag; if it stays because no derived value changed, say that in the report.

## Running the requirements check

The requirements check is `as-check.py`, run by file path through `run_python`. Build its path from the folder you read this `SKILL.md` from (the path you passed to `run_python`, or the base directory a Skill tool gave you). That folder belongs to the installed plugin version, so never hard-code it or reuse one from an earl

# /as:rhino-setup

Before acting, read the [host contract](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md), this component's [declaration](host-contract.json) (`skill:rhino-setup`) and the mode profiles it references in the [shared catalog](../../corpus/host-contracts.json). Declarations are requirements, not proof of access or permission.

<!-- architecture-studio:harness-compatibility -->
Use the [host adapter](../../docs/host-adapters.md) for native invocation.

## Outcome

A confirmed working connection (tools present, a document open, units known, a script round-trip proven) or the exact user action that is missing.

## Procedure

1. **Tools.** Look for Rhino's tools (`run_python`, `get_context`), from the AI panel or a connected agent. If absent, stop and give the user this action: "Open a document in Rhino 9 and make this request in its AI panel. To use an agent outside Rhino, such as Claude Code in a terminal, run `MCPConnect` once in Rhino 9 and install it for your agent, then run `MCPStart` on the open model and start a new agent session." Arch Studio never installs, registers or configures anything.
   Also note whether the hosted Arch Studio MCP is connected too: its workflow tools are named `as_*` and come from an MCP server other than Rhino's (in Claude Code, `mcp__<server>__as_...`). Only the tool list says this; do not call those tools and do not compare versions.
2. **Document.** `get_context` must answer with the open document. Then one `run_python` script reads `__rhino_doc__`, `Rhino.RhinoApp.Version` and `sys.platform`: Rhino version, operating system (`darwin` is macOS, `win32` is Windows), units, name, path, live object count, top-level layers. If the version is below 9, report that the skills are written for Rhino 9. These values hold for this turn only; a later turn reads them again.
3. **Smoke test** only when the user asked to verify: add one named point on a layer `Rhino Setup Check`, read it back, delete it and the layer, and report both steps. Never touch other objects. Run this script as written in one `run_python` call; it is tested in Rhino 9 and keeps a `Rhino Setup Check` layer that existed before. Layer calls with one string argument (`Layer(name)`, `Layers.Add(name)`, `Layers.FindByFullPath(name)`) fail there with "No overload".

```python
import Rhino
d = __rhino_doc__
NAME = "Rhino Setup Check"
made = d.Layers.FindByFullPath(NAME, -1) < 0
if made:
    layer = Rhino.DocObjects.Layer()
    layer.Name = NAME
    d.Layers.Add(layer)
index = d.Layers.FindByFullPath(NAME, -1)
attr = Rhino.DocObjects.ObjectAttributes()
attr.LayerIndex = index
attr.Name = "rhino-setup check point"
gid = d.Objects.AddPoint(Rhino.Geometry.Point3d(0, 0, 0), attr)
obj = d.Objects.FindId(gid)
print("added:", obj is not None and obj.Attributes.Name == attr.Name and obj.Attributes.LayerIndex == index)
print("point deleted:", d.Objects.Delete(gid, True))
print("layer deleted:" if made else "layer kept, it existed before:", d.Layers.Delete(index, True) if made else NAME)
```

## Report

Tools found or not, Rhino version and operating system, document name or "untitled", units, object count, smoke-test result, and the next user action if anything is missing. On Windows, only when your context has no Arch Studio startup line (the line naming `as-rhino-index.md` and the lessons folder), tell the user to install Git for Windows and start a new panel session: Claude Code runs the plugin's startup hook in Git Bash. When that line is there, the hook ran: say nothing about Git for Windows, the startup line or pointing to the index. Complete under the [completion contract](../../docs/completion-reporting.md). If the hosted Arch Studio MCP is also connected, add this line: "The hosted Arch Studio MCP is also connected; use the Arch Studio plugin or the MCP, not both (README, Two editions)."

skills.name: rhino-thinline
skills.desc: Drawing conventions for black and white vector sheets from a Rhino 9 model: a line hierarchy, line styles, hatch by material on the cut faces of details, labels and leaders, detail tags, a title block, the sheet layout, a tamper-proof request record and a checked PDF. Use when the user asks for a line drawing, drawing sheet or black and white export from a Rhino model; for an axonometric, load rhino-axon, which chooses the view and loads this skill's library. Not for construction documents, coloured images or renders; line weights and hatch patterns are working conventions.
skills.body:
---
name: rhino-thinline
description: "Drawing conventions for black and white vector sheets from a Rhino 9 model: a line hierarchy, line styles, hatch by material on the cut faces of details, labels and leaders, detail tags, a title block, the sheet layout, a tamper-proof request record and a checked PDF. Use when the user asks for a line drawing, drawing sheet or black and white export from a Rhino model; for an axonometric, load rhino-axon, which chooses the view and loads this skill's library. Not for construction documents, coloured images or renders; line weights and hatch patterns are working conventions."
---

# /as:rhino-thinline

Before acting, read the [host contract](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md), this component's [declaration](host-contract.json) (`skill:rhino-thinline`) and the mode profiles it references in the [shared catalog](../../corpus/host-contracts.json). Declarations are requirements, not proof of access or permission.

<!-- architecture-studio:harness-compatibility -->
Use the [host adapter](../../docs/host-adapters.md) for native invocation. Requires Rhino 9 with an open document and its `run_python` tool. **Plugin-only:** the sheet and its PDF check use `scripts/as-sheet.py`, `as-sheet-core.py` and `as-pdf-check.py` from the installed plugin's folder ([Rhino skill helpers](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md#rhino-skill-helpers)); through hosted MCP instruction delivery this skill is not available. If you cannot find this skill's folder on disk, stop and tell the user to install the plugin. In the Rhino AI panel, there is no Skill tool: read this file and its references by path with `run_python`.

## Outcome

A layout in the open document and a one-page vector PDF, read back and passed by the PDF check, in pure black and white, with the sheet's limits said plainly in the reply.

This skill owns how the sheet looks: weights, styles, hatch, annotation, layout, the request record and the PDF. It never chooses a view. The view for an axonometric (camera and projection, exclusions and crop, occlusion, joint and detail-cut selection, the building lock) is [rhino-axon](../rhino-axon/SKILL.md), which draws the linework and hands it here ([the handoff](../rhino-axon/references/views.md#the-linework-handoff)).

## Invariants

1. **The main drawing is the focus.** Details serve it and are sized to the space left.
2. **The line hierarchy is the drawing.** Filled forms hide what is behind them, and silhouette, edge and receding lines are separate thin strokes on separate layers ([linework](references/linework.md)).
3. **Black and white only.** Strokes and hatch are black on white; colour language in notes fails the check. The linework is static: after a model change, the view regenerates it.
4. **Detail leaders are orthogonal only,** and a label's leader ends in a dot on its part.
5. **Hatch only real cut faces, by material.** Cut faces are hatched in the round details only; a cut-away in the main drawing is drawn in outline, not hatched. The patterns are working conventions, not checked against a standard; say so on request.
6. **Measure, do not estimate.** Text boxes, margins and scale are read from the document.
7. **Verify the PDF by parsing it, and an empty parse is a failure.** A sheet is not done until `as-pdf-check.py` passes.
8. **Line weights are provisional.** They were accepted on screen and have not been proven on paper. Say so in every report until a printed sheet accepts them.
9. **Never change a check's threshold; fix the sheet.** The checks' limits are fixed in the library, not arguments. When a check fails, move or resize what it names.
10. **Never delete a failure record or request to pass a check; report what could not be placed.** Every label, locator and detail you ask for is recorded, and `check_sheet` fails each one the sheet does not show, and fails an edited or deleted record. A label that finds no clear leader stays a failure until it is drawn; if you stop there, name each unplaced item in the report.

## Procedure

Read the [lessons](#lessons) after setup and before asking; write them after the report.

1. **Setup.** If the Rhino tools are absent, follow [rhino-setup](../rhino-setup/SKILL.md) for the user action.
2. **Ask** in one `ask_user` batch only what is open: drawing, scale, sheet size, details, title text. Each question carries what it asks about, with your proposal as the first option ("Keep 1/4\" = 1'-0\""), since the question pane covers the chat; never refer to text shown behind it. Scale and title are open unless the request gives them: ask for both; when nobody can answer, choose them and say in the report that you chose them. Propose a scale in the document's unit system: an imperial architectural scale (such as 1/4" = 1'-0", 1:48) for a document in feet or inches, a metric one (such as 1:50) for a metric document, and write it that way in the title block. Details follow from the drawing, not the reverse. Where `ask_user` is not available (an agent connected to Rhino from outside it), ask the same questions in chat, with the same options, and end the turn.
3. **Load the library** by file path. For an axonometric, load [rhino-axon](../rhino-axon/SKILL.md)'s `as-axon.py` instead: it loads this library first, and the sheet script then has both. For linework from another view, load this one alone. Build the path from the folder you read this `SKILL.md` from, which belongs to the installed plugin version; never hard-code it or reuse one from an earlier version:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-sheet.py"
S = {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P}
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), S)
```

4. **Build in this order** with one script per step, following [sheets](references/sheets.md): `new_sheet` for the layout, border and title column (axon's `setup_sheet` calls it); the view's linework (axon's `main_linework`); annotation and callouts; details (axon's `cut_detail`); title block and table. Annotation goes after linework, so it draws on top.
   - Label components with `place_label`: it puts each label in the clear paper nearest its part, with a straight leader ending in a dot on the part, and refuses a leader that would cross the drawing. When a label or detail cannot be placed and `check_sheet` names it, the fix is in the view: follow [rhino-axon](../rhino-axon/SKILL.md)'s steps, never edit the model.
5. **Review** the whole sheet, then zoom each new element. Each round of review in the source session found something new. With no viewport, run `S["preview_sheet"](d, page, "<absolute path>.png")`: look at the PNG if you can open images, cropping it to zoom. It also prints and returns a text summary (the closest rings, leaders and text with their distances in mm, what sits nearest the field's edge, and any detail ring that is mostly empty); act on that when you cannot see the image.
6. **Check the sheet** with `S["check_sheet"]`, passing the drawing field (margins are checked against a fixed 10 mm); loaded through rhino-axon, it is the full check and also takes the main linework root, the main detail and its scale. Then export with `S["export_pdf"]` and run the PDF check:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-pdf-check.py"
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_PDF": "<absolute path>.pdf", "AS_PDF_SIZE": [914.4, 609.6]})
```

## Lessons

This skill learns locally. Before planning, read its lessons and the firm rules; at the end of every run, write what the run learned. The folder is the one the Arch Studio startup line names; the tags, the privacy rule and promotion are in [lessons](../as-rhino-lessons.md), read once per session.

```python
P = "<absolute path of the skills folder, the parent of this skill's folder>/as-rhino-lessons.py"
```

# /as:rhino-thinline

Before acting, read the [host contract](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md), this component's [declaration](host-contract.json) (`skill:rhino-thinline`) and the mode profiles it references in the [shared catalog](../../corpus/host-contracts.json). Declarations are requirements, not proof of access or permission.

<!-- architecture-studio:harness-compatibility -->
Use the [host adapter](../../docs/host-adapters.md) for native invocation. Requires Rhino 9 with an open document and its `run_python` tool. **Plugin-only:** the sheet and its PDF check use `scripts/as-sheet.py`, `as-sheet-core.py` and `as-pdf-check.py` from the installed plugin's folder ([Rhino skill helpers](../../docs/host-harness-contract.md#rhino-skill-helpers)); through hosted MCP instruction delivery this skill is not available. If you cannot find this skill's folder on disk, stop and tell the user to install the plugin. In the Rhino AI panel, there is no Skill tool: read this file and its references by path with `run_python`.

## Outcome

A layout in the open document and a one-page vector PDF, read back and passed by the PDF check, in pure black and white, with the sheet's limits said plainly in the reply.

This skill owns how the sheet looks: weights, styles, hatch, annotation, layout, the request record and the PDF. It never chooses a view. The view for an axonometric (camera and projection, exclusions and crop, occlusion, joint and detail-cut selection, the building lock) is [rhino-axon](../rhino-axon/SKILL.md), which draws the linework and hands it here ([the handoff](../rhino-axon/references/views.md#the-linework-handoff)).

## Invariants

1. **The main drawing is the focus.** Details serve it and are sized to the space left.
2. **The line hierarchy is the drawing.** Filled forms hide what is behind them, and silhouette, edge and receding lines are separate thin strokes on separate layers ([linework](references/linework.md)).
3. **Black and white only.** Strokes and hatch are black on white; colour language in notes fails the check. The linework is static: after a model change, the view regenerates it.
4. **Detail leaders are orthogonal only,** and a label's leader ends in a dot on its part.
5. **Hatch only real cut faces, by material.** Cut faces are hatched in the round details only; a cut-away in the main drawing is drawn in outline, not hatched. The patterns are working conventions, not checked against a standard; say so on request.
6. **Measure, do not estimate.** Text boxes, margins and scale are read from the document.
7. **Verify the PDF by parsing it, and an empty parse is a failure.** A sheet is not done until `as-pdf-check.py` passes.
8. **Line weights are provisional.** They were accepted on screen and have not been proven on paper. Say so in every report until a printed sheet accepts them.
9. **Never change a check's threshold; fix the sheet.** The checks' limits are fixed in the library, not arguments. When a check fails, move or resize what it names.
10. **Never delete a failure record or request to pass a check; report what could not be placed.** Every label, locator and detail you ask for is recorded, and `check_sheet` fails each one the sheet does not show, and fails an edited or deleted record. A label that finds no clear leader stays a failure until it is drawn; if you stop there, name each unplaced item in the report.

## Procedure

Read the [lessons](#lessons) after setup and before asking; write them after the report.

1. **Setup.** If the Rhino tools are absent, follow [rhino-setup](../rhino-setup/SKILL.md) for the user action.
2. **Ask** in one `ask_user` batch only what is open: drawing, scale, sheet size, details, title text. Each question carries what it asks about, with your proposal as the first option ("Keep 1/4\" = 1'-0\""), since the question pane covers the chat; never refer to text shown behind it. Scale and title are open unless the request gives them: ask for both; when nobody can answer, choose them and say in the report that you chose them. Propose a scale in the document's unit system: an imperial architectural scale (such as 1/4" = 1'-0", 1:48) for a document in feet or inches, a metric one (such as 1:50) for a metric document, and write it that way in the title block. Details follow from the drawing, not the reverse. Where `ask_user` is not available (an agent connected to Rhino from outside it), ask the same questions in chat, with the same options, and end the turn.
3. **Load the library** by file path. For an axonometric, load [rhino-axon](../rhino-axon/SKILL.md)'s `as-axon.py` instead: it loads this library first, and the sheet script then has both. For linework from another view, load this one alone. Build the path from the folder you read this `SKILL.md` from, which belongs to the installed plugin version; never hard-code it or reuse one from an earlier version:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-sheet.py"
S = {"__rhino_doc__": __rhino_doc__, "AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P}
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), S)
```

4. **Build in this order** with one script per step, following [sheets](references/sheets.md): `new_sheet` for the layout, border and title column (axon's `setup_sheet` calls it); the view's linework (axon's `main_linework`); annotation and callouts; details (axon's `cut_detail`); title block and table. Annotation goes after linework, so it draws on top.
   - Label components with `place_label`: it puts each label in the clear paper nearest its part, with a straight leader ending in a dot on the part, and refuses a leader that would cross the drawing. When a label or detail cannot be placed and `check_sheet` names it, the fix is in the view: follow [rhino-axon](../rhino-axon/SKILL.md)'s steps, never edit the model.
5. **Review** the whole sheet, then zoom each new element. Each round of review in the source session found something new. With no viewport, run `S["preview_sheet"](d, page, "<absolute path>.png")`: look at the PNG if you can open images, cropping it to zoom. It also prints and returns a text summary (the closest rings, leaders and text with their distances in mm, what sits nearest the field's edge, and any detail ring that is mostly empty); act on that when you cannot see the image.
6. **Check the sheet** with `S["check_sheet"]`, passing the drawing field (margins are checked against a fixed 10 mm); loaded through rhino-axon, it is the full check and also takes the main linework root, the main detail and its scale. Then export with `S["export_pdf"]` and run the PDF check:

```python
P = "<absolute path of this skill's folder>/scripts/as-pdf-check.py"
exec(compile(open(P).read(), P, "exec"), {"AS_SCRIPT_FILE": P, "AS_PDF": "<absolute path>.pdf", "AS_PDF_SIZE": [914.4, 609.6]})
```
